title: From DARPA AIxCC to Microsoft FORGE Lab: Lessons Building Hyperscale AI Code Scanning Tools

speakers.name: Taesoo Kim
speakers.affiliation: VP, Security Research, Microsoft (also professor at Georgia Tech, on leave, per the Microsoft blog author page shown)

thesis: AI vulnerability discovery has moved from a research demonstration (DARPA's AI Cyber Challenge, AIxCC) to production at hyperscale (Microsoft's multi-model agentic scanning harness, MDASH), and the hard problems are now cost per audit, deciding when to stop spending tokens, and feeding the expensive validation and remediation stages back into finding, which is why Microsoft's FORGE Lab (Frontier Offensive Research and Generative Exploitation) is pivoting to exploitability as the organizing signal.
summary: Kim opens with the DARPA AI Cyber Challenge (AIxCC) as the ChatGPT moment for security: a $30 million competition his Team Atlanta won, with the winning system, a long technical report, a systematization-of-knowledge paper and the OSS-CRS (open-source cyber reasoning system) code and CRSBench benchmark all released. He says AIxCC showed AI can do professional-level cyber tasks at about $150 per task, and that frontier labs then productized the idea (Big Sleep, CodeMender, Aardvark, Claude Code Security, Codex Security Review). He shows open source skepticism (curl's Daniel Stenberg) turning into acceptance and Microsoft's monthly Patch Tuesday CVE count climbing sharply after March 2026. He says five Team Atlanta members joined Microsoft and, within five months, shipped MDASH, a multi-model, multi-agent scanning harness with five stages: prepare, scan, validate, dedup, prove. He explains four design ideas: turn search into decision problems, use the function as the orchestration unit, funnel candidates through increasingly expensive validation, and enrich source with LLM-written taint and bounds annotations. He reports 229 Windows and Hyper-V CVEs fixed, including 38 remote code execution bugs, and a Linux kernel exploit-generation experiment. He closes with three shifts (scale and cost, reasoning economics, a continuous learning loop), all pushing toward exploitability.
argument: DARPA AIxCC showed that LLM-driven systems can find and patch real vulnerabilities at professional level for roughly $150 per task, and the frontier labs productized that within about a year.
Skepticism from open source maintainers and the security community flipped to adoption, visible in a steep rise in Microsoft CVEs fixed per Patch Tuesday after March 2026.

MDASH makes AI scanning work in production by forcing agents through an explicit pentester-style workflow, with function-level decision questions, shared annotated context, and multi-persona validation before expensive proving.

With discovery solved, the bottlenecks are cost per audit, knowing how many tokens are enough, and the much costlier triage, validation and deployment stages, so findings must be ranked and learned from.

FORGE Lab therefore prioritizes exploitable bugs: reason about exploitation early, spend tokens on exploitation reasoning, and use exploit techniques as the feedback loop, demonstrated on automatic exploit generation against the Linux kernel.

claims.claim: AIxCC concluded that AI can conduct professional-level cyber tasks at about $150 per successful task.
claims.evidence: Stated as a statistic from the competition; the slide repeats $150 / task with no breakdown of how it was computed.

claims.claim: Team Atlanta won AIxCC, scoring 392.76 against 219.35 for the second-place team.
claims.evidence: Final scoreboard on the slide with columns for correct submission rate, vulnerability discovery, program repair, SARIF assessment and bundle score; Atlantis also leads the cumulative score chart across the rounds.

claims.claim: Microsoft fixes about 70 CVEs in a typical Patch Tuesday, and the count rose to over 1,100 by July 2026, with a sharp rise after March 2026.
claims.evidence: Line chart of CVEs fixed per month (MSRC / Patch Tuesday): a flat baseline near 69 to 80 through February 2026, then 1,142 in July 2026. The speaker said about 1600 aloud, which the slide does not support.

claims.claim: MDASH was built and announced within five months of five Team Atlanta members joining Microsoft, and is now adopted internally and commercialized as part of the Defender product.
claims.evidence: Timeline slide showing the MDASH announcement at Microsoft Build; the Defender commercialization claim is spoken only.

claims.claim: Forcing agents through an explicit multi-stage pentester workflow (prepare, scan, validate, dedup, prove), with termination after each stage, beats loosely coupled skills layered on a general agent harness by giving control over token spend per stage.
claims.evidence: Architecture description and Q&A answer; no head-to-head comparison against skill-based tools was shown.

claims.claim: More concrete, narrower questions (a function, a bug class, a line) give higher success and fewer hallucinations than asking an agent to find bugs in a repo, but are hard to scale by hand.
claims.evidence: Experience reported from building the tool, illustrated by a ladder of copilot prompts from whole repo down to a line-level integer overflow question.

claims.claim: Inlining LLM-generated taint, data-flow and bounds annotations into function source drastically reduced false positives, and sharing the annotated source across the 100-plus agents cuts redundant reasoning.
claims.evidence: Speaker's description of tinkering with comments and then automating it with an LLM; the slide shows an annotated SQLite-style function with categories (Vuln, Bounds, Flow, Control, Safety, Meta). No false-positive rates were given.

claims.claim: MDASH on a multi-model configuration scores above single frontier models (Claude Mythos Preview, GPT-5.5, GPT-5.4) on an unnamed benchmark, despite using older-generation models at announcement time.
claims.evidence: Scatter plot of success rate against model release date with MDASH circled at roughly 88 to 90 percent; the benchmark is not named on the slide or aloud.

claims.claim: MDASH-reported fixes on Windows and Hyper-V total 229 critical or important CVEs, including 38 remote code execution bugs at an average CVSS of 7.7, growing from 16 in the May launch cohort to 89 in October.
claims.evidence: Stacked bar chart by month with critical and important counts: May 16, June 10, July 27, August 35, September 52, October 89; the speaker said about 200.

claims.claim: In an automatic exploit generation experiment on the Linux kernel, about 5 percent of MDASH static reports reproduced as crashes (600-plus at about $3.6 per PoC), and about 1.8 percent of those crashes became exploits, yielding 11 local privilege escalations at $10 or more per exploit.
claims.evidence: Results slide with token-cost and time charts over 182 matched crash cases and a small set of mitigated LPE cases, labeled GPT-5.5; most crashes depend on non-default configuration so are not security concerns.

claims.claim: Cost per stage rises steeply (finding less than triaging, much less than validation, far less than deployment), so the expensive later stages should feed back into cheaper, better-ranked finding.
claims.evidence: Shift 3 slide stating the cost ordering; no cost data given. Spoken estimate is weeks to months for the post-discovery work.

claims.claim: Binary diffing of published patches to find and exploit the fixed bug now takes drastically less time because of AI, so organizations must push updates to customers with extreme care.
claims.evidence: Speaker answer to an audience question; no timing data.

claims.claim: Frontier-lab safeguards increasingly block binary analysis and exploit-related requests, so many practitioners use open-weight models such as Kimi and GLM, which Kim says are extremely capable for this work.
claims.evidence: Speaker's observation from recent model cards and practice; no comparison shown.

frameworks.name: MDASH pipeline
frameworks.description: Multi-model agentic scanning harness with five stages. Prepare builds a per-repo knowledge base (threat model, repo map, call graph, CVEs and patches mined from Git). Scan runs 100-plus specialized agents per bug type, choosing 3 to 5 relevant ones per function. Validate has Models A, B and C debate as different personas and vote, two of three. Dedup collapses duplicates. Prove generates a proof of concept in three stages (self-contained, reachability harness, fuzzing) in a Docker build with sanitizers, then optional patch generation (AutoFix) and patch validation with audit.

frameworks.name: Four core design ideas
frameworks.description: Idea 1: turn the search problem into decision problems by asking narrower questions. Idea 2: use the function as the unit of orchestration, with each function checked by parallel agents per bug class. Idea 3: scale by funneling through static self-dispute, multi-perspective debate, reachability evaluation, dynamic constraint concretization, and finally a PoC, with cost rising at each step. Idea 4: enrich source with LLM-generated inline annotations for taint and boundaries.

frameworks.name: Three shifts
frameworks.description: Shift 1, from frontier capability to scale: cut tokens per audit with small, specialized or multiple models. Shift 2, from token consumption to reasoning economics: security is roughly the tokens spent on security reasoning, so decide what is enough and spend cost-effectively. Shift 3, validation and remediation as a continuous learning loop: rank bugs, reuse past lessons. FORGE restates each shift around exploitation.

frameworks.name: Hybrid static and dynamic spectrum
frameworks.description: Atlantis started from dynamic fuzzing and added LLMs; MDASH started from static LLM reasoning and added tooling and proving; both move toward a hybrid with better applicability and low false positives.

offense: Patch diffing: with AI, the time to reverse a published patch (including binaries) into a working exploit has dropped drastically, shrinking the window between patch release and attacker exploitation.
AI reduces the cost to attack, so low-skill attackers become powerful and the scope of required auditing expands.
Automatic exploit generation against the Linux kernel: from patch, report or crash to local privilege escalation or remote code execution, yielding 11 LPEs from 600-plus reproduced crashes.
Frontier models resist binary analysis plus exploitation requests, pushing offensive users toward open-weight models.
defense: Run an explicit staged pipeline (prepare, scan, validate, dedup, prove) rather than a single general agent, so token budget can be set per stage.
Ask narrow decision questions per function and bug class, run them in parallel, and let agents flag suspicious sites before any exploitation work.
Pre-annotate source with LLM-generated taint and boundary information and share it across all agents to cut false positives and redundant reasoning.
Validate with multi-persona debate across different model backends (developer, defender, attacker) and a two-of-three vote before proving.
Require a PoC or reachability evidence for high-assurance findings; allow developers to consume the earlier suspicious-site output for pre-commit scans.
Mine Git history and CVE or MSRC tags in commits for variant analysis across the codebase.
Keep the pipeline model agnostic and run a benchmark suite whenever a new model ships; use powerful models for high-stakes targets and cheaper models for broad scans.
Coordinate disclosure of upstream findings through community channels such as LF Akrites rather than posting to public lists.
takeaways: As a design to test, budget AI code scanning by stage: spend cheaply on broad per-function discovery and reserve expensive models and dynamic proving for candidates that survive static debate.
Measure cost per audit and when to stop, and check in your own runs whether token spend tracks assurance, which the talk argues without cost data.
On an assertion with no timing data, expect patch-to-exploit time for your shipped software to shrink, and plan patch rollout speed and customer update enforcement accordingly.

Check whether validation and deployment, not finding, dominate your cost and are where false positives hurt most; if so, invest in ranking and exploitability triage. The talk asserts this without cost data.
Do not assume frontier-model access for offensive-adjacent security work; test open-weight models and keep your pipeline model-agnostic.
limits: Speaker acknowledged most Linux crashes depend on non-default configurations and are not security concerns.
Cost and infrastructure, not capability, now limit adoption because few organizations need or can afford frontier-level scanning.
Post-discovery work remains expensive and manual, taking weeks to months.
The design assumes bugs keep being introduced; the speaker noted that if AGI arrives, that premise may change.
critique: The benchmark behind the model comparison chart is not named, and MDASH is compared as a multi-model system against single models, so the chart does not isolate the value of the pipeline design.
Claims about false-positive reduction from annotations and multi-persona debate come with no rates, ablations or comparisons to simpler pipelines.

The CVE counts include only fixed, shipped Windows and Hyper-V bugs by cohort; there is no denominator for scanned code, triage effort, rejected findings or how many findings were severe versus low value.
The Patch Tuesday chart is attributed to AI-driven discovery in general, not just MDASH, and the speaker's spoken figure (about 1600) conflicts with the slide (1,142).
The $150 per task figure is repeated without definition of task, success or how it generalizes beyond the AIxCC challenge projects.
MDASH is a product of the speaker's company, Microsoft.
The Q&A answer on pipeline erosion argues for staged control; no comparison against simpler agent-plus-strong-model setups was shown.
qa: Q: How long to reverse engineer a Windows patch, and can open models do this locally? A: Binary diffing used to be slow; with AI the time to analyze and exploit drops drastically, so even large vendors must be careful pushing updates to customers. Open-weight models such as Kimi and GLM work very well, and many people use them because frontier models block binary analysis plus exploitation.

Q: What context goes into the annotation pass and the per-function pass, and do agents have tools to look up definitions? A: Static analysis (taint tracking and a CodeQL-backed code graph) feeds the LLM, which writes inline comments on each function; all agents then share the same annotated source.

Q: How do you think about variance and about verifying patches? A: Answered variant analysis only: agents use CVE or MSRC tags in commits to generalize where similar bugs may exist; patch verification was not addressed.

Q: How much of the pipeline must be retested per model release? A: A large benchmark pipeline retests model combinations; the system is model agnostic, so models are interchangeable, with powerful models for high-stakes targets and cheaper ones for large-scale scans.

Q: Does a stronger model erode the benefit of a segmented pipeline, and what does it do to cost? A: Open-source scanners such as skill-based harnesses are loosely coupled; forcing explicit stages gives control over token spend per stage. The speaker did not claim the pipeline remains optimal as models improve.

key_frames.caption: MDASH architecture: Prepare, Scan, Validate, Dedup, Prove stages with 100-plus agents per bug type, three-model debate vote and PoC generation stages.
Monthly MDASH CVEs fixed on Windows and Hyper-V, totaling 229 including 38 RCEs, rising from 16 to 89 per month.
Linux kernel automatic exploit generation results with conversion rates, per-case costs and times, and cost charts.
Funnel of increasingly expensive validation from static self-dispute to dynamic PoC.
Three shifts framing the hybrid static and dynamic future: scale, reasoning economics, continuous learning loop.

signal.reason: The talk reports production figures (229 Windows and Hyper-V CVEs fixed, a Linux kernel exploit-generation experiment) and a five-stage scanning pipeline design, with no ablations or rates for several design claims.

caveats: The captions say Entropy, Mithos and R Vark; the slides say Anthropic, Mythos and Aardvark, and this record uses the slides.
The speaker said about 200 vulnerabilities and about 1600 Patch Tuesday fixes; the slides say 229 MDASH CVEs and 1,142 for July 2026, and this record uses the slides.
Speaker said the Windows team adopted MDASH in CI/CD since April; the CVE chart labels the first cohort May launch.
The Linux kernel chart text is small and values were read from a mid-resolution slide capture; the 11 LPE count is from the slide and speech while the right chart shows 6 mitigated LPE cases.
The benchmark in the model-comparison chart is not named, and chart values are estimated from point positions.
Slide title reads Microsoft Security FORGE Lab: The Next Journey, while the listed talk title is From DARPA AIxCC to Microsoft FORGE Lab.
Speaker affiliation appears as VP, Security Research on the slide and Vice President, Agentic Security on the Microsoft author page.
